strengths: Addresses an important gap in evaluating personalization in search-augmented LLMs with a well-motivated and timely problem
Innovative dataset construction using authentic long-term user histories (2,870 sessions over 3 weeks from 30 diverse annotators) rather than synthetic personas
Novel evaluation framework combining scalar scores with diagnostic feedback on four well-chosen criteria (need alignment, content depth, tone, explanation style)
Strong meta-evaluation demonstrating high agreement with human judgments (Pearson 0.853, Spearman 0.857) and showing empirically that diagnostic feedback significantly improves evaluator quality

Comprehensive systematic analysis revealing concrete, actionable insights about user context construction (query-aware contexts outperform static; selected histories outperform raw; profiles outperform raw histories)
Excellent attention to privacy, ethics, and reproducibility with multi-stage de-identification, diverse annotators (Shannon equitability 0.91), and extensive documentation of methods and prompts
Case studies effectively demonstrate how diagnostic feedback provides detailed diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses in model responses
weaknesses: Limited scale (only 30 users, 150 queries, ~600 R-J pairs) severely constrains generalizability; findings may be specific to this small annotator cohort without evidence of broader applicability

Circular evaluation methodology: gold information is extracted from gold responses and evaluated against model responses, artificially biasing recall metrics toward confirming the gold response's completeness

Heavy and concerning dependency on GPT-5 for user context construction (Sections 4.2, C.3), oracle history selection (C.4), and evaluation (Section 3.4), making it difficult to disentangle results about personalization from model-specific artifacts

Meta-evaluation shows modest absolute performance without feedback (Pearson correlations of 0.374 for need alignment, 0.356 for content depth), and the framework appears to heavily rely on in-context examples to work well

Unclear practical impact: no model exceeds 60/100 average score despite comprehensive experiments; key findings (query-aware > static, selected > raw) are intuitive rather than surprising; no proposed methods emerge
Bi-encoder retrieval limitations (nDCG@10 = 0.082) are presented as limitations rather than solved; only one retriever model tested; query expansion helps but doesn't solve the underlying problem
Potential annotator biases: all 30 users are active daily users of Google Search and generative AI; 3-week collection window is short for capturing stable preferences; all used Google accounts

Incomplete experimental design: Table 4 shows selected configurations rather than complete factorial design; no statistical significance testing in results; GPT-5 reasoning effort always set to 'high' without justification
Limited task diversity: only 4 task types pre-selected from Search-Arena without justifying why these are the most important information-seeking scenarios for personalization
The evaluator design relies on complex manually-crafted prompts with no sensitivity analysis or ablation of prompt components; few-shot approach may not generalize beyond in-domain query-user pairs

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem in evaluating personalization of search-augmented LLMs, filling a concrete evaluation gap
Exemplary data collection: 3-week long-term human annotation with 30 diverse annotators (22+ professional domains, 60+ interests, Shannon equitability=0.91) ensuring representativeness
Rich annotation beyond simple labels: diagnostic feedback explaining scores, explicit gold information needs, multi-stage response-judgment pairs, and both search/chat histories (not just QA)
Thorough meta-evaluation demonstrating evaluator reliability: Pearson/Spearman correlations ~0.85 with humans, ablations showing feedback critical, validation with open-weight models (Appendix A.1)

Comprehensive systematic analysis with well-designed ablations (history usage, query awareness, history selection, context form) across 6 models, oracle experiments clearly identifying history inference as main bottleneck
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: extensive appendices with implementation details, prompts, case studies, dataset statistics, and clear ethical considerations with IRB approval
Practical insights: query-aware selective profiles outperform raw/static histories; reasoning models sensitive to search quality; findings actionable for system design
weaknesses: Dataset scale severely limited: only 150 queries total (30 users × 5 queries), restricting practical utility for training/evaluation; proposed LLM augmentation (A.6) not demonstrated
Evaluation methodology not novel: few-shot LLM-based evaluation follows Zheng et al. (2023) and Liu et al. (2023); application to personalization is incremental
Heavy circularity and dependence: GPT-5 used as evaluator, gold response generator, rubric generator, and profile generator, creating single point of failure; generalization beyond this model unclear
Artificial data collection: 3-week collection period with dedicated accounts is not natural long-term usage; no analysis of whether collection duration is sufficient for capturing stable preferences

Limited novelty of findings: query-aware > static profiles (intuitive), selective > full history (expected from IR), structured > raw profiles (unsurprising); no surprising insights to advance personalization research
History retrieval analysis weak: Table 5 shows ~38% recall at top-10 (nDCG 0.38); bi-encoder limitations acknowledged but not addressed; oracle uses expensive GPT-5 calls
Incomplete personalization analysis: four criteria narrow in scope; no user-segment analysis; case studies anecdotal; lacks dimensions like user satisfaction over time or trust
Statistical rigor issues: no inter-annotator agreement reported (only self-review); no significance testing; practical significance of correlation differences unexplored; limited error analysis

strengths: Realistic and diverse user dataset collected through long-term engagement with authentic chat and search histories from 30 annotators across 22+ professional domains
Comprehensive multi-stage annotation pipeline with quality control measures and validation through detailed examples (Figure 3, Tables 14-15)
Strong meta-evaluation demonstrating high alignment between GPT-5-based evaluator and human judgments (Pearson 0.847, Feedback accuracy 0.881); supplemented by open-weight model validation
Systematic ablation studies thoroughly examining four dimensions of user context construction with clear evidence that query-aware selective profiles substantially improve performance
Novel contribution of diagnostic feedback framework paired with scores, providing actionable signals for understanding personalization failures
Thorough ethical practices including multi-stage privacy review, informed consent, fair compensation ($50 + 3 months AI Pro), participant autonomy, and IRB approval
Excellent reproducibility documentation with complete prompts, annotation guidelines, dataset statistics, and commitment to release code and data
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (30 users, 150 queries) reduces statistical robustness and generalization potential; scalability claims in Appendix A.6 via LLM augmentation remain largely speculative

Core bottleneck identified but unaddressed: oracle experiment (Appendix A.4) shows models achieve 83.47 need alignment with explicit preferences but only 59.07 with history-based inference, yet no solutions proposed
Modest technical novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (multi-level annotation, LLM-based evaluation); no new methods proposed for improving personalization
Restricted to 4 task types (analysis, guidance, recommendation, explanation); generalization to other information-seeking scenarios (factual lookup, comparison) unclear

Heavy reliance on proprietary models (GPT-5 for evaluation, Gemini for annotation) raises reproducibility and availability concerns; LLM-based PII detection and manual de-identification privacy procedures lack formal validation
Privacy procedures depend on subjective manual inspection and may miss sophisticated re-identification attacks; effectiveness of de-identification not formally validated
Some findings about user context (query-aware, selective, structured) are intuitive rather than surprising; limited methodological advancement
Key findings (oracle experiment in A.4, reasoning model sensitivity in A.5) buried in appendices despite importance; paper at 30 pages is lengthy for the contribution level
